scenes.visual: Title card 'Why the Pea Didn't Starve' over two pots, a lush pea and a small oat. Reuses the first film's COLOUR MAP for both films: phosphate BLUE dots; nitrate and ammonium GREEN dots; nitrogen gas PALE GREY paired dots labelled 'N2'; phloem movement a GOLD arrow; Casparian strip a DARK RED band; carbon payment ORANGE tokens; soil tan, roots cream, fungal threads WHITE. Every number appears only as on-screen text. No molecular structures: labelled blocks and cartoons, all marked 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Nitrogen gas makes up most of the air around every plant. So why can a pea use it, while an oat beside it starves?
scenes.visual: A pea plant and an oat plant side by side, surrounded by drifting PALE GREY 'N2' pairs. The oat droops; the pea is green. Question mark between them.
scenes.narration: Nitrogen gas makes up most of the air around every plant. So why can a pea use it, while an oat beside it starves?

scenes.tts: The first film showed that how far a nutrient moves shapes how a plant reaches it. But form matters too. Nitrogen gas is everywhere, yet no plant enzyme can use it.
scenes.visual: Brief replay of the first film's end-card line. Then PALE GREY 'N2' pairs bounce off a leaf, labelled 'no plant enzyme can use it'.
scenes.narration: The first film showed that how far a nutrient moves shapes how a plant reaches it. But form matters too. Nitrogen gas is everywhere, yet no plant enzyme can use it.

scenes.tts: At an experiment station in Bernburg, Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth tested this in pots. They grew peas and oats in washed, sterilised sand.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Hellriegel and Wilfarth, Bernburg, 1888'. Rows of glass pots fill with pale sand; pea seedlings in one row, oat seedlings in another.
scenes.narration: At an experiment station in Bernburg, Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth tested this in pots. They grew peas and oats in washed, sterilised sand.

scenes.tts: Every pot got a base solution with the other mineral nutrients, but no nitrogen. So any extra nitrogen had to come from what they added, or from the air.
scenes.visual: A watering can labelled 'base solution: every mineral except nitrogen' passes over the pots; mineral tiles drip in, the 'N' tile crossed out.
scenes.narration: Every pot got a base solution with the other mineral nutrients, but no nitrogen. So any extra nitrogen had to come from what they added, or from the air.

scenes.tts: Now think about what that means. If every plant relied on soil nitrogen alone, none could end up with more nitrogen than its seed held.
scenes.visual: A pea seed glows with a small bar labelled 'nitrogen in seed'. A dashed ceiling line extends from it across all the pots, labelled 'the most it could hold here without another nitrogen source'.
scenes.narration: Now think about what that means. If every plant relied on soil nitrogen alone, none could end up with more nitrogen than its seed held.

scenes.tts: Some oat pots got no nitrogen at all. Others got measured doses of nitrate. The oats grew only as far as the nitrate they were given allowed.
scenes.visual: Oat pots in a row receive increasing GREEN nitrate doses, labelled 'none', 'low', 'medium', 'high'. The oats grow taller in step with the dose (schematic).
scenes.narration: Some oat pots got no nitrogen at all. Others got measured doses of nitrate. The oats grew only as far as the nitrate they were given allowed.

scenes.tts: Peas with nothing added did the same, and stayed small. But some peas got a little extract shaken from field soil. Those grew well.
scenes.visual: Pea pots: one labelled 'no extract' stays small; another labelled 'live soil extract' gets a few drops from a flask of brown soil water and grows tall.
scenes.narration: Peas with nothing added did the same, and stayed small. But some peas got a little extract shaken from field soil. Those grew well.

scenes.tts: Their roots formed swellings called nodules. And the plants ended up with far more nitrogen than their seeds had held. That extra nitrogen came from the air.
scenes.visual: Cutaway of the tall pea's roots: round nodules appear. A bar 'nitrogen in seed' is small; a bar 'nitrogen at harvest' rises far above it, labelled 'gained from the air' (schematic bars).
scenes.narration: Their roots formed swellings called nodules. And the plants ended up with far more nitrogen than their seeds had held. That extra nitrogen came from the air.

scenes.tts: One more set of pots got soil extract that had been heated first. Will those peas form nodules, and gain nitrogen?
scenes.visual: A third pea pot, labelled 'heated extract', receives drops from a flask over a flame. Question card holds.
scenes.narration: One more set of pots got soil extract that had been heated first. Will those peas form nodules, and gain nitrogen?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: No. No nodules, and no nitrogen gained. A living agent in the soil, tied to the nodules, was needed.
scenes.visual: The heated-extract pea stays small with smooth roots. Three pots line up like the lesson figure: 'no extract', 'live extract', 'heated extract'; only the middle has nodules. Label 'a living agent from soil'.
scenes.narration: No. No nodules, and no nitrogen gained. A living agent in the soil, tied to the nodules, was needed.

scenes.tts: That agent is a group of bacteria called rhizobia. They enter the root. Inside nodule cells, they change into bacteroids.
scenes.visual: Zoom into one nodule: rod-shaped bacteria labelled 'rhizobia' enter root cells and swell into packed shapes labelled 'bacteroids'.
scenes.narration: That agent is a group of bacteria called rhizobia. They enter the root. Inside nodule cells, they change into bacteroids.

scenes.tts: Bacteroids hold an enzyme called nitrogenase. It turns nitrogen gas into ammonia, a form the plant can use. The pea itself makes no nitrogenase.
scenes.visual: A labelled block 'nitrogenase (bacteroid)' takes in PALE GREY 'N2' pairs and releases GREEN dots labelled 'ammonia', which flow out into the plant. A pea cell with label 'makes no nitrogenase'.
scenes.narration: Bacteroids hold an enzyme called nitrogenase. It turns nitrogen gas into ammonia, a form the plant can use. The pea itself makes no nitrogenase.

scenes.tts: The pea pays for this. Sugar made in its leaves travels down to the nodule. There it is turned into malate, which fuels the bacteroids.
scenes.visual: ORANGE tokens labelled 'sucrose' travel from a leaf down the stem to the nodule, where they turn into ORANGE tokens labelled 'malate' and enter the bacteroids.
scenes.narration: The pea pays for this. Sugar made in its leaves travels down to the nodule. There it is turned into malate, which fuels the bacteroids.

scenes.tts: So the trade is carbon for nitrogen. Oats have no nodules. They depend mainly on nitrate and ammonium already in the soil.
scenes.visual: Two-way trade loop on the nodule: ORANGE tokens in, GREEN ammonia out. Beside it the oat root, no nodules, takes up only GREEN soil dots.
scenes.narration: So the trade is carbon for nitrogen. Oats have no nodules. They depend mainly on nitrate and ammonium already in the soil.

scenes.tts: Nitrogen gas is all around the pea, but in a form it cannot use. So it pays carbon to a partner that can use it.
scenes.visual: Recap: the three pots, the nodule zoom, and the ORANGE-for-GREEN loop side by side.
scenes.narration: Nitrogen gas is all around the pea, but in a form it cannot use. So it pays carbon to a partner that can use it.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex. LINE: 'A form the plant cannot use can be bought from a partner.'
